text: Selling to a local trader/collector (ឈ្មួញ / អ្នកប្រមូលទិញ) -- who comes to the farm and handles transport/onward marketing -- is often practical for Preah Vihear smallholders with scattered farms, difficult wet-season roads, small volumes, and no truck or storage. A lower farm-gate price (តម្លៃនៅចម្ការ) than a distant market quote is not automatically exploitation -- it reflects the trader's transport, labor, aggregation, and risk. The right comparison is net return after transport, loading, grading, storage, and spoilage that the farmer would otherwise pay, not the raw quoted price. Traders solve a real smallholder problem: aggregating many farmers' small quantities (e.g. 300+500+700 kg) into a commercially useful shipment. This applies across rice, cassava, maize, cashew, vegetables, and livestock. For highly perishable vegetables especially, farm-gate speed can outweigh a higher but delayed market price, since unsold produce loses value to heat and wilting. For livestock, a sick animal should never be sold to a trader just to avoid losing its value -- unexplained illness or mortality is an animal-health issue to resolve before normal marketing continues. During the wet season, muddy roads make farm-gate collection more valuable since the trader absorbs the transport difficulty; during the dry season, easier transport creates more chances to compare buyers, but farmers may face pressure to sell quickly for cash. Compare offers from more than one buyer when practical, clarify the unit/quality grade being used, and record price and payment received. Do not invent a current local price, buyer, or crop/breed a farmer hasn't confirmed.
